paragraphs.heading: Where spacetime breaks down
paragraphs.text: A gravitational singularity, also called a spacetime singularity or just a singularity, is a theoretical state in which gravity is expected to grow so strong that spacetime itself fails. Because of that, a singularity is not part of ordinary spacetime at all, and you cannot say where or when it is. General relativity, today's theory of gravity, has no complete and exact definition of one. It can be pinned down either by a measure of curvature going to infinity or by a so-called geodesic being incomplete, which means it comes to an end after a finite span of time.

paragraphs.heading: A warning sign in the maths
paragraphs.text: Many physical theories contain mathematical singularities, where some quantity in the equations becomes infinite or grows without limit. This usually signals that something is missing from the theory. In classical field theories, special relativity among them, spacetime acts as a background, so a singularity can still be placed at a point. In general relativity it is harder, because spacetime itself is what stops making sense.

paragraphs.heading: Inside every black hole
paragraphs.text: According to general relativity, any object that collapses past its Schwarzschild radius becomes a black hole with a singularity inside. In a black hole that does not spin, the singularity is a single point; in a spinning one it spreads into a ring lying in the plane of rotation. Either way it has zero volume and holds all of the black hole's mass, so it can be thought of as infinitely dense. Because it sits behind an event horizon, no outside observer can ever be affected by it, and at no moment can one say for certain that it has formed.

paragraphs.heading: Falling in
paragraphs.text: Anyone falling into a black hole that neither spins nor carries charge cannot avoid the singularity once past the event horizon. On the way down, growing tidal forces tear them apart, a process sometimes called spaghettification. At the end they are crushed into an infinitely small point. If the inside of the black hole has been disturbed, for instance by matter or radiation falling in, space near the singularity would instead oscillate chaotically.

paragraphs.heading: Spinning and charged black holes
paragraphs.text: In a black hole that spins or carries charge, the singularity can in principle be avoided. Pushing these solutions as far as they go hints at leaving through the black hole into another spacetime, as if it were a wormhole. This stays purely theoretical, since any disturbance would destroy that route. Paths that loop back into one's own past also seem possible around what is called the Kerr singularity, raising causality puzzles like the grandfather paradox.

paragraphs.heading: Do they really exist
paragraphs.text: Nobody knows whether real black holes contain singularities. Some physicists think they do not, and that their appearance shows general relativity breaking down and the need for a better grasp of quantum gravity. Others think the problem can be solved within today's physics, while Kip Thorne and Charles Misner are among those who expect some singularities to survive even with quantum effects. Models without them exist too: in loop quantum gravity, a black hole has large but not infinite curvature and density at its centre, and the fuzzball model from string theory has neither a singularity nor an event horizon.

paragraphs.heading: The Big Bang
paragraphs.text: General relativity also predicts that the universe began, at the Big Bang, as a singularity of infinite density and temperature. Classical theories of gravity are not expected to hold under such extreme conditions, and a quantum description will likely be needed.
